« Ce n’est pas juste un gym, c’est une m: “It’s not just a gym, it’s a home” – In Côte-des-Neiges, the youth of Philo-Boxe describe their refuge
À Côte-des-Neiges, Philo-Boxe offre aux: In Côte-des-Neiges, Philo-Boxe gives young people a place to belong, where boxing and philosophy foster inclusion and confidence.
La projection du documentaire et la disc: The documentary screening and discussion held at the Institut national de la recherche scientifique brought together young people, researchers and community workers to talk about the Philo-Boxe experience. Photo: Édouard Desroches
Je me suis intéressé à Philo-Boxe parce: I became interested in Philo-Boxe because the organization sits at the crossroads of several issues we regularly follow at La Converse: youth, a sense of belonging, violence prevention and the role of community organizations in Montréal neighbourhoods. When I heard about the screening of the documentary Boxe, discipline et philosophie, l’autre combat, I saw a chance to understand what such a space concretely means for the young people who use it.
Pour réaliser ce reportage, j’ai assisté: To report this story, I attended the documentary screening and the discussion that followed at the Institut national de la recherche scientifique (INRS). I spoke with several participants, including Wided and Mohamed, two young people involved in Philo-Boxe, as well as the organization’s founder, Karim Coppry. I also consulted demographic data on Côte-des-Neiges and interviewed researcher Leslie Touré Kapo to place Philo-Boxe’s challenges in the broader context of community funding and the needs of young people in working-class neighbourhoods.
Mon intention n’était pas de réaliser le: My intention was not to write a profile of an organization or to assess its effectiveness, but to understand why young people describe this place as a “second family” and what that tells us about the needs they face. I also sought to put the funding issues raised during the evening into perspective by comparing them with an independent analysis of the community sector.
<strong>Dans Côte-des-Neiges, un quartie: In Côte-des-Neiges, a Montréal neighbourhood often associated with poverty, violence and exclusion, one organization has spent several years trying to build something else: a space where young people can box, think, debate and simply be themselves. Through the voices of Wided, Mohamed and other teenagers, this report tells how Philo-Boxe became much more than a sports club: a place of belonging. But as needs grow, the organization must also contend with the fragility of a community network short on resources.
Le visage de Wided apparaît à l’écran. A: Wided’s face appears on the screen. Seated in a corner of the Tiers-lieu room at the Institut national de la recherche scientifique (INRS), the young woman briefly looks away from the documentary to observe the audience. Her gaze sweeps the room as if looking for a reaction, an emotion, perhaps a judgment.
Quelques secondes plus tôt, on l’entenda: A few seconds earlier, she could be heard speaking in Boxe, discipline et philosophie, l’autre combat, a documentary made in collaboration with the organization Exeko that presents the approach Philo-Boxe has developed with young people in Côte-des-Neiges.
Née à Montréal dans une famille d’origin: Born in Montréal to a family of Egyptian origin, Wided is 18 and boxes, a sport still largely associated with boys. During the screening, her image comes back several times.
Lorsque les lumières se rallument, elle: When the lights come back on, she takes a seat on a platform beside another young person from the organization, Mohamed Diallo. In front of a room full of community workers, researchers, partners and residents, she agrees to talk about her journey.
La jeune femme ne cherche ni à impressio: The young woman doesn’t try to impress or embellish her story. She tells La Converse: “My life is a bit complicated.” Then, in a few sentences, she describes what Philo-Boxe means in her daily life: “When I’m sad outside and I climb the stairs of Philo-Boxe, I’m always happy as soon as I walk into the space.”
Devant le public, elle résume tout cela: In front of the audience, she sums it all up in one simple sentence: “It’s not just a gym. It’s a home.”
Si Philo-Boxe trouve autant d’écho auprè: If Philo-Boxe resonates so strongly with young people, it’s also because of where it is. With more than 100,000 residents, Côte-des-Neiges is one of the most populous and diverse areas of Montréal.<l1> Nearly a third of its population is between 18 and 34</l1>, a higher proportion than the Montréal average. In an area marked by significant social inequalities, community organizations are often essential anchors.
<strong>Une deuxième famille au cœur de: A second family in the heart of Côte-des-Neiges
Dans un quartier comme Côte-des-Neiges,: In a neighbourhood like Côte-des-Neiges, where dozens of cultural communities live side by side and where community organizations often play a front-line role, Philo-Boxe has spent several years trying to create a different kind of space for teenagers.
Fondé par Karim Coppry, l’organisme prop: Founded by Karim Coppry, the organization offers free boxing classes to young people aged 12 to 18. But boxing is only part of the equation. The other, lesser-known component is philosophy.
Les participants prennent part à des ate: Participants take part in discussion workshops where they debate social issues, test their views against each other, and learn to present their arguments and listen to those of others. It’s an unusual formula – and it gives the organization its name.
« Beaucoup de gens se demandent ce qu’on: “A lot of people wonder what we are,” explains Karim Coppry. “Are we boxing? Are we community work? In reality, we’re a bit of both.”
L’organisme se définit aussi comme un «: The organization also defines itself as a “third space” for young people: neither school nor home, but a place where they can simply be themselves and<l1> box for the future.</l1>
Pour Mohamed Diallo, qui a 18 ans et fré: For Mohamed Diallo, who is 18 and has been coming to Philo-Boxe for a few months, what sets the place apart isn’t primarily the sport. “The word that best defines Philo-Boxe is: family,” he tells La Converse. And he adds later: “Even if you disappear for a few months because of personal problems, when you come back, nobody asks you any questions. You just get a big smile.”
Pour Wided, cette famille choisie est ar: For Wided, this chosen family arrived at a time when she needed one. Her words come out with a disarming frankness. She talks about a lack of support, difficulties piling up over the years and a feeling of loneliness that often stays with her. Even when she smiles, that worry still seems present. “My experience with boys was never good. I didn’t feel respected.”
Puis, elle revient à son premier pas : a: Then she goes back to her first step: at the start, she was simply curious. Her brother already boxed, and she wanted to try the sport too. But it was a friend she met at school who convinced her to walk through the organization’s doors. Quickly, the experience took on another dimension. “Here,” she says, “everyone supports you. Everyone listens to your voice. Everyone is always there for you.”
Il lui arrive même de se rendre à l’orga: She sometimes even goes to the organization without putting on gloves. “Sometimes I just come to chill,” she says with a smile. Behind the humour, the message is simple: some young people come looking not just for an activity, but for a place to breathe.
Cette fonction dépasse le simple cadre d: This role goes beyond sport alone. In the documentary, Leslie Touré Kapo, an assistant professor at INRS who specializes in exclusion and youth in urban settings, says Philo-Boxe represents a form of community innovation that has become harder to bring about today. In his view, the organization plays a decisive role in young people’s well-being and development, but also in the vitality of Côte-des-Neiges as a whole.
<strong>Boxer avec ses gants, réfléchir: Boxing with gloves on, thinking with others
À première vue, la boxe et la philosophi: At first glance, boxing and philosophy seem to belong to two opposite worlds, but at Philo-Boxe, the two disciplines complement each other. Mohamed even sees it as one of the project’s great strengths. “Philosophy is something that lets you question everything.”
Selon lui, l’adolescence est une période: He says adolescence is a time when you try to figure out who you are and what place you hold in the world. “When you’re young, you’re searching inside yourself.” The philosophy workshops then become a space where young people can express their opinions, debate sometimes sensitive subjects and hear views different from their own. For Wided, philosophy and boxing answer the same need: to understand what she’s going through and to learn to defend herself in ways other than anger.
Karim Coppry estime que cette combinaiso: Karim Coppry believes this combination is one of the keys to the project. Boxing teaches discipline, perseverance and how to manage effort. Philosophy helps develop reflection, listening and self-confidence.
Cette approche n’empêche pas les jeunes: This approach doesn’t stop the young people from performing athletically. Quite the opposite. Last April, at the provincial Gants de Bronze competition, one of Philo-Boxe’s athletes, Kilian-Alexis Galeano, won the gold medal in the under-60 kg category for under-22s. The club came home from the competition with three other medals: two silver and one bronze. When footage of the competition appears on screen, the room applauds. The young people, seated in the front row, savour the recognition and exchange knowing glances.
<strong>Quand la prévention doit constam: When prevention constantly has to justify itself
Malgré les témoignages enthousiastes des: Despite the young people’s enthusiastic accounts, the organization’s future remains fragile. Throughout the evening, one question comes up again and again: funding. Like many Quebec community organizations, Philo-Boxe operates amid limited resources and permanent uncertainty. “The hardest thing is seeing that youth is still not treated as a priority,” says Karim Coppry.
Il parle des demandes de financement ref: He talks about rejected funding applications, repeated approaches to funders and the feeling of constantly having to prove the value of the work being done.
Pour le professeur Leslie Touré Kapo, ce: For Professor Leslie Touré Kapo, this reality goes well beyond Philo-Boxe’s situation. “When we talk about young people in working-class neighbourhoods, we’re also talking about young people who face issues with housing, employment, poverty and discrimination,” he explains. “The scientific literature has shown for a long time that the needs are significant.”
Selon lui, le problème n’est pas seuleme: In his view, the problem isn’t only the level of funding, but also the conditions for accessing it. Over the years, organizations have had to cope with increasingly bureaucratic funding programs and ever-heavier accountability requirements. “You constantly have to justify your existence and demonstrate your impact,” he sums up.
Le chercheur estime également que la gén: The researcher also believes the spread of project-based funding weakens community work over the long term. “Because we operate project by project, we always have to reinvent ourselves,” he says. “That heightens competition between organizations and contributes to their exhaustion.”
Depuis plusieurs mois, le mouvement Le c: For several months, the movement Le communautaire à boutte! has stepped up actions to denounce the chronic underfunding of Quebec’s community sector,<l1> a stranglehold that, among other things, prevents crime prevention.</l1> In Wided and Mohamed’s neighbourhood, about a hundred community workers and volunteers took part on March 25 in a symbolic blockade of chemin de la Côte-des-Neiges to demand better support for the sector.
Pour les organismes jeunesse, la questio: For youth organizations, the issue is particularly sensitive. The results of their work are often hard to measure in the short term. They sometimes show up as what doesn’t happen: a young person who doesn’t drop out, distress that finds a listening ear, a conflict that doesn’t escalate.
Cette question de la prévention traverse: This question of prevention has run through Côte-des-Neiges for a long time. After the<l1> death of teenager Jannai Dopwell-Bailey, stabbed in front of his school in 2021</l1>, his family publicly called for more spaces for the neighbourhood’s young people. His mother said she wanted a place where teenagers could meet, play, create and simply be together.
Quatre ans plus tard, les témoignages en: Four years later, the accounts heard during the evening devoted to Philo-Boxe offer a concrete glimpse of what such a place can mean when it exists.
Vers la fin de la discussion, une person: Toward the end of the discussion, someone in the audience asks a question that causes a slight unease. “What would happen if Philo-Boxe no longer existed?” Karim Coppry prefers to let the young people answer. Mohamed speaks first. He says he believes the people gathered in the room would find a way to rebuild something. That the ideas would survive. That the spirit of the project would carry on.
Puis vient le tour de Wided. Son ton cha: Then it’s Wided’s turn. Her tone changes. The emotion becomes visible. “Since day one, I’ve felt like I was in a family.” She says she has already thought about this possibility when the organization was going through financial difficulties. “If it closes, I don’t know what I’m going to do.” She searches for her words, then continues: “They really gave me a second family.” For the organization’s staff, that answer is probably worth more than an evaluation report or a performance indicator.
Au fond, c’est peut-être cela que racont: In the end, perhaps that is what the documentary is telling. Behind the funding debates and the statistics are very real young people looking for their place.
Comme tout organisme communautaire, Phil: Like any community organization, Philo-Boxe doesn’t claim to solve on its own the difficulties faced by the neighbourhood’s young people, but those who come here clearly find much more than a gym.
À la fin de la soirée, alors que les dis: At the end of the evening, as conversations continue in the INRS Tiers-lieu, Wided’s sentence keeps echoing. “It’s not just a gym. It’s a home.”
